title: What Dissolving Carbon Does To Shells
paragraphs: Roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide human activity has released into the atmosphere never stayed there.
It crossed the sea surface and dissolved.
That transfer is usually described as a favor, the ocean taking on part of the problem and slowing the warming of the air.
The description is accurate as far as it goes.
What it leaves out is that the ocean does the favor by chemistry, and the chemistry does not leave the water unchanged.
The first steps are simple enough to write on a napkin.
Carbon dioxide gas dissolves in seawater, and a small fraction of it combines with water to form carbonic acid.
Carbonic acid is weak and unstable, and it promptly sheds a hydrogen ion, leaving a bicarbonate ion.
A much smaller fraction of that bicarbonate sheds a second hydrogen ion and becomes a carbonate ion.
In pure water that sequence would simply make the water more acidic.
Seawater is not pure water, and the part that matters begins one step later.
Seawater already carries a standing stock of carbonate ions, and carbonate is an eager scavenger of hydrogen.
Nearly every hydrogen ion released by dissolving carbon dioxide is intercepted by a carbonate ion already there, and the two combine into another bicarbonate ion.
The bookkeeping is worth following slowly.
Total dissolved inorganic carbon goes up.
Bicarbonate goes up sharply.
Hydrogen ion concentration goes up slightly, which is what a falling pH records.
And carbonate ion concentration goes down.
Adding carbon to seawater subtracts carbonate from it, and that inversion is the engine of the whole problem.
Carbonate matters because many marine organisms build their hard parts out of it.

A calcifier draws a calcium ion and a carbonate ion out of solution and lays the pair down as calcium carbonate: a coral skeleton, a clam shell, the chalky plates of a single celled alga, the spines of a sea urchin.
Scarcer carbonate means a crystal that once assembled readily must be coaxed into place.
Chemists summarize that difficulty with one number, the saturation state, written as omega.
It compares the actual product of calcium and carbonate concentrations against the product at equilibrium with solid calcium carbonate.
Where omega exceeds one the water is supersaturated and a crystal left in it tends to grow.
Where omega is below one the water is undersaturated and an unprotected crystal tends to dissolve.
Calcium is abundant and varies little, so omega rises and falls with carbonate.
Deeper water is colder, under greater pressure, and loaded with carbon dioxide from matter decomposing as it sinks, so omega falls with depth.
The depth at which it passes through one is the saturation horizon.
Above that boundary shells are thermodynamically safe; below it the only thing keeping a living animal's shell intact is its own covering of tissue or organic film.
The horizon sits at very different depths in different basins.
In the North Atlantic, where surface water sinks relatively recently and carries little accumulated respiratory carbon, it lies thousands of meters down.
In the North Pacific, whose deep water is the oldest in the world ocean and has spent centuries collecting respired carbon dioxide, it can sit within a few hundred meters of the surface.
That boundary is not fixed, and it has been moving in one direction.
As atmospheric carbon dioxide works into the upper ocean, the depth at which omega falls below one shoals, migrating upward toward the light.
In parts of the North Pacific the change has been measured in tens of meters over a few decades.
Where seasonal upwelling already drags deep water onto a continental shelf, the two can meet, and water corrosive to shell arrives in the shallow, sunlit places where larvae are trying to build one.
Calcium carbonate is also not a single material.
It crystallizes in more than one arrangement, and two dominate marine biology: calcite and aragonite.
They share an identical chemical formula and differ in the internal geometry of the crystal, and that geometry sets the solubility.
Aragonite is roughly half again as soluble as calcite in seawater, so in any water column the aragonite saturation horizon sits shallower than the calcite horizon.
An organism's choice of crystal is not a matter of taste.
It decides which portion of the ocean is hospitable to it at all.
The division cuts across the tree of life almost arbitrarily.
Reef building corals lay down aragonite.
So do pteropods, the small swimming snails called sea butterflies, eaten by everything from herring to whales.
Coccolithophores, the single celled algae whose plates turn stretches of the North Atlantic milky in bloom season, build calcite, as do the foraminifera whose shells accumulate on the seafloor.
Many molluscs use both: an adult oyster's outer shell is largely calcite, while the first shell a larval oyster assembles is aragonite.
A third form, calcite with magnesium substituted into part of the crystal, is more soluble still than aragonite, and it is what coralline algae and sea urchins use.
Here the most common phrase in public discussion of the subject does damage.
The ocean is repeatedly said to be turning to acid.
It is not.
Surface seawater has a pH near 8.1, comfortably on the alkaline side of neutral, and it has fallen from roughly 8.2 since the industrial era began.
No plausible emissions trajectory takes the open ocean below 7.
Acidification names a direction of travel, not a destination, in the way a bath cooling from scalding to merely hot is cooling.
The imprecision is not harmless: a reader who pictures a sea of vinegar and later learns the truth may throw out the subject entirely.
But the correction is no reprieve.
Shells do not wait for pH 7.
They answer to a saturation state that can cross below one while the water is still alkaline.
Nor do organisms sit passively in the water around them.
Most calcifiers do not precipitate skeleton directly out of seawater.
They wall off a small internal space, a calcifying fluid held between tissue and skeleton, and pump hydrogen ions out of it, holding its pH well above the pH outside.
These mechanisms are genuinely effective.

Laboratory populations of some corals, some coccolithophores and several crustaceans have held calcification rates steady under carbon dioxide levels far beyond what the coming century should deliver, and a few have raised them.
Such results are sometimes reported as evidence that the concern was overblown.
They are better read as evidence that calcification has a price and that the price is climbing.
Pumping protons against a steeper gradient is expensive, and the energy must come from somewhere in an animal that is also feeding, growing, defending itself and reproducing.
The trade shows up in measurements that rarely make headlines: shells of normal size but lower density, larvae slower to reach settlement, adults that keep their skeletons and release fewer eggs.

A shellfish hatchery on the Pacific Northwest coast can lose most of a batch of oyster larvae when upwelled, undersaturated water enters its intake, not because the water dissolves them but because they cannot build fast enough in the window when they must build.
The picture is uneven rather than uniform, and careful accounts of it resist a single verdict.
Response varies between species, between populations of one species, and between seasons.

Seagrass meadows and kelp forests pull carbon dioxide out of the water during daylight and can lift the local saturation state enough to shelter the animals among them, then give much of it back after dark.
Estuaries swing across a wider chemical range in a day than the open ocean is projected to cross in a century, and the organisms there are built for the ride.
None of this contradicts the chemistry.
It means the chemistry is a boundary condition ecology plays out against, not a script it has to read.

To see what happens when that boundary condition shifts quickly, the usual place to look is an interval about 56 million years ago, preserved in the geological record and known as the Paleocene Eocene Thermal Maximum.
A large quantity of carbon entered the ocean and atmosphere, the planet warmed by several degrees, and the seafloor recorded the consequence with unusual clarity.
In deep sea sediment cores the pale carbonate ooze that had piled up for millions of years gives way abruptly to a band of brown clay, then returns over the next tens of thousands of years.
Carbonate did not stop being produced.
It dissolved on the seafloor as the saturation horizon rose through the sediment, and a substantial fraction of deep dwelling foraminifera species went extinct.
The event is instructive, and it is also asked with some regularity to carry more weight than it can bear.
It shows that the carbonate system responds to a large carbon injection as theory predicts, and that recovery is slow, since the processes that restore balance work over tens of thousands of years.
What it does not show is the present rate.

Estimates place that ancient release on the order of several thousand years, against roughly two centuries for the modern one, and rate is nearly the whole question, because the ocean's slow buffers only help if they are given time.
Nor can the record resolve a decade: sediment accumulates slowly and burrowing animals stir it, so a fifty year event can smear into invisibility.
The pH values come from proxies such as boron isotopes in fossil shells, which carry real uncertainty.
And the species that filled that ocean are not the species in this one.
What survives the caveats is a narrower claim than the headlines make and a firmer one.
The chemistry is not in dispute: carbon dioxide entering seawater raises dissolved carbon and lowers carbonate, and it is doing so faster than anything the record can resolve.
The saturation horizons are rising, and that is measured rather than modeled.

What remains open is the biology, meaning which organisms will pay the climbing price out of reserves they can spare, which will pay it out of growth and reproduction they cannot, and which will simply move.

questions.stem: According to the passage, aragonite differs from calcite in that aragonite
choices: carries magnesium substituted into part of its crystal
has a chemical formula unlike that of calcite
dissolves more readily in seawater than calcite does
is the material of coccolithophore plates and foraminifera shells
stays saturated to a greater depth in the water column

proof.quote: roughly half again as soluble as calcite in seawater

questions.why: Paragraph 8 makes the whole comparison turn on solubility. The two forms share a formula, differ in the internal geometry of the crystal, and aragonite is roughly half again as soluble in seawater.
distractorNotes: That describes the third form the passage names later, magnesium bearing calcite, not aragonite.
The passage says the two share an identical chemical formula and differ only in crystal geometry.
Those are the calcite builders the passage lists, which is the opposite grouping.
This reverses the result: because aragonite is more soluble, its saturation horizon sits shallower, not deeper.

questions.stem: The passage attributes the shallow saturation horizon of the North Pacific mainly to
choices: the unusually high pressure of that particular ocean basin
the long residence of its deep water, which has collected respired carbon dioxide
the seasonal upwelling that drags deep water up onto the continental shelf each summer
the number of aragonite building organisms living in its surface water
a calcium concentration much lower there than in other basins

proof.quote: has spent centuries collecting respired carbon dioxide

questions.why: Paragraph 6 contrasts the two basins directly. North Pacific deep water is the oldest in the world ocean and has spent centuries collecting carbon dioxide from decomposition, so its saturation horizon can sit within a few hundred meters of the surface.
distractorNotes: Pressure rises with depth everywhere, so it cannot explain why one basin differs from another.
Upwelling is what carries that water onto a shelf, not what made the water corrosive in the first place.
The passage never connects how many calcifiers live above a spot to how deep its horizon lies.
The passage says calcium is abundant and varies little, which is why omega tracks carbonate instead.

questions.stem: The passage names which organisms as builders of the magnesium bearing form of calcite?
choices: reef building corals
pteropods, the small swimming snails of polar water
coccolithophores
foraminifera
coralline algae and sea urchins

proof.quote: it is what coralline algae and sea urchins use

questions.why: Paragraph 9 closes by naming a third crystal form, calcite with magnesium substituted into part of it, and says coralline algae and sea urchins are the organisms that use it.
distractorNotes: Corals are listed as aragonite builders at the start of that paragraph.
Pteropods are grouped with corals as aragonite builders.
Coccolithophores are given as builders of ordinary calcite.
Foraminifera are also placed in the ordinary calcite group.

questions.stem: According to the passage, deep sea sediment cores record the ancient warm interval as
choices: a thickening of the pale carbonate ooze
an abrupt band of brown clay set between layers of carbonate ooze
a dense layer of intact foraminifera shells
a slow darkening spread evenly across many millions of years of accumulated sediment
a gap in which no sediment accumulated at all

proof.quote: gives way abruptly to a band of brown clay

questions.why: Paragraph 14 describes the core signature plainly. Pale carbonate ooze that had piled up for millions of years gives way abruptly to brown clay, then returns over the following tens of thousands of years, because the carbonate was dissolving on the seafloor.
distractorNotes: This reverses what happened: the ooze stops and clay takes its place.
The passage says the opposite, that a substantial fraction of deep dwelling foraminifera species went extinct.
The passage calls the change abrupt, with the recovery, not the onset, taking tens of thousands of years.
Sediment kept accumulating. What changed is that the carbonate in it dissolved.

questions.stem: The passage gives the pH of present day surface seawater as
choices: slightly below 7
exactly 7, the neutral point
about 7.5, down from roughly 8 over the last century
near 8.1, down from roughly 8.2
near 8.2 and essentially unchanged

proof.quote: a pH near 8.1
it has fallen from roughly 8.2

questions.why: Paragraph 10 gives both numbers. Surface seawater sits near 8.1, down from roughly 8.2 since the industrial era began, which keeps it on the alkaline side of neutral.
distractorNotes: That would put seawater on the acid side, which the passage says no plausible trajectory reaches.
Neutral is exactly what the passage says surface seawater is not.
Both numbers are wrong and they overstate the shift the passage actually reports.
The passage reports a drop of about a tenth of a unit, so the value has not held steady.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, "shoals" most nearly means
choices: gathers into dense groups
becomes sandy and shallow, like a sandbar
splits apart into separate layers
slows to a gradual crawl
moves nearer to the surface

proof.quote: shoals, migrating upward toward the light

questions.why: Paragraph 7 is tracking a depth. The boundary is migrating upward toward the light, measured in tens of meters over a few decades, so the word means climbing toward the surface.
distractorNotes: That is the fish sense of the word, and nothing in the sentence concerns animals grouping together.
A shoal as a sandbar is a different sense, and the sentence is about a chemical boundary, not sediment.
The passage describes one boundary moving, not a boundary dividing in two.
The sentence measures distance, tens of meters, rather than any rate of motion being slow.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 12, "expensive" most nearly means
choices: scarce and hard to obtain
demanding of the animal's energy
costly in terms of money and trade
elaborate in its design
damaging to nearby tissue

proof.quote: the energy must come from somewhere

questions.why: Paragraph 12 defines the word in the very next clause: the energy must come from somewhere in an animal that is also feeding, growing, defending itself and reproducing. The cost is metabolic.
distractorNotes: Scarcity in this passage belongs to carbonate in the water, not to the pumping the word describes.
The monetary sense is the dictionary one, but the sentence is about where an animal's energy comes from.
The passage is not commenting on how intricate the mechanism is.
The passage never says the pumping harms tissue, only that it draws on a limited energy supply.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which statement about a parcel of seawater that has taken up extra carbon dioxide?
choices: It holds more dissolved carbon overall yet less of the ion a shell builder needs
It holds less dissolved carbon, because the carbon departs as bicarbonate
It holds more carbonate than before, since carbonate is one of the products of the reaction
It has turned acidic and will dissolve any shell that is placed into it
Its calcium concentration has fallen in step with its carbonate concentration

proof.quote: Total dissolved inorganic carbon goes up.
carbonate ion concentration goes down
many marine organisms build their hard parts out of it

questions.why: Paragraph 3 walks the bookkeeping through one line at a time. Total dissolved inorganic carbon rises and bicarbonate rises sharply, while carbonate, the ion a calcifier draws on, goes down.
distractorNotes: Total dissolved inorganic carbon goes up in that paragraph, and bicarbonate is where most of it ends up rather than leaving.
Carbonate is consumed in the passage's account, because it mops up the freed hydrogen ions.
The water stays alkaline, and whether a shell dissolves depends on saturation state rather than on the water being acidic.
The passage says calcium is abundant in seawater and varies little.

questions.stem: A species is found in the laboratory to hold its shell growth rate unchanged under high carbon dioxide. Based on the passage, the author would most likely treat that result as
choices: proof that the species is untouched by the change in seawater chemistry
probably a measurement error, given what the chemistry predicts
leaving open what the species gave up to hold that rate
evidence that the species has permanently adapted to any future condition
a result that will hold equally for every species sharing its habitat

proof.quote: calcification has a price and that the price is climbing
shells of normal size but lower density

questions.why: Paragraph 12 handles exactly this case. The author accepts steady laboratory rates and reads them as a cost met somewhere else, showing up in shell density, larval timing, or eggs released.
distractorNotes: The author treats a steady rate as a sign that a cost is being met elsewhere, not as a sign of no effect.
The author accepts these laboratory results and calls the mechanisms behind them genuinely effective.
The passage ties compensation to circumstances such as food supply rather than to a permanent solution.
The passage says response varies between species and even between populations of one species.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central point of the passage?
choices: Added carbon dioxide lowers the carbonate shell builders need, a settled chemical result whose biological effects remain open
The ocean is on course to become acidic enough that marine shells will dissolve outright in open water within a century
Marine calcifiers have evolved mechanisms that will carry them through the change without meaningful cost to growth or reproduction
The record of an ancient warming interval shows in fine detail what the coming century will do to the ocean and its marine life
Concern about seawater chemistry has been exaggerated, largely by the imprecise language that reporters and scientists use in public

proof.quote: Adding carbon to seawater subtracts carbonate from it
raises dissolved carbon and lowers carbonate
What remains open is the biology

questions.why: The passage runs one chemical result, less carbonate, out through organisms, depth, popular wording, coping mechanisms and the fossil record. The closing paragraph states the balance directly: the chemistry is not in dispute, the biology is what remains open.
distractorNotes: The passage denies this outright, saying no plausible trajectory takes the open ocean below 7 and tying shell trouble to saturation state instead.
Coping mechanisms are described, but the passage insists they carry a cost that is climbing.
The passage says the ancient record cannot show what happens at the present rate.
The author does criticize the phrasing, then refuses to let the correction count as reassurance.

questions.stem: The author's main purpose in the paragraph that takes up the phrase about acid is to
choices: show that popular reporting on seawater chemistry is on the whole trustworthy and precise
argue that pH is a misleading way to describe any chemical change in a solution
correct a common misstatement while denying that the correction is cause for relief
establish that the open ocean will eventually fall below neutral on the pH scale
explain why a cooling bath and a warming ocean behave in much the same way

proof.quote: It is not.
But the correction is no reprieve.

questions.why: Paragraph 10 spends half its length correcting the slogan and the other half refusing the comfort that correction might offer, closing with shells answering to a saturation state while the water is still alkaline.
distractorNotes: The paragraph faults the popular phrasing rather than defending it.
The author uses pH values freely and objects only to one careless slogan.
The passage states the opposite, that no plausible emissions trajectory takes the open ocean below 7.
The bath appears only as an analogy for direction of travel, not as a claim about baths.

questions.stem: How does the paragraph on the energy cost of calcification relate to the paragraph on internal chemical control that comes just before it?
choices: It supplies the laboratory evidence for the mechanism just described
It grants the evidence and rereads what that evidence means
It disputes the accuracy of the measurements just reported
It shifts the subject from living organisms to the fossil record
It restates the earlier point using a different set of organisms

proof.quote: sometimes reported as evidence that the concern was overblown
They are better read as evidence

questions.why: Paragraph 11 reports that some corals, coccolithophores and crustaceans hold calcification rates steady. Paragraph 12 does not deny those results, it rereads them as evidence that calcification has a price and that the price is climbing.
distractorNotes: The laboratory evidence sits in the earlier paragraph, and the later one reads it differently.
The author accepts the measurements and questions only the conclusion drawn from them.
The fossil record does not enter the passage until two paragraphs later.
The later paragraph adds a new claim about cost rather than repeating the old one.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the claim that the ocean is turning to acid is best described as
choices: accepting it as a simplification that serves the public well
dismissing the whole subject as overstated
indifferent to how the chemistry gets described
alarmed that the phrase badly understates the danger
correcting the wording but insisting the worry stands

proof.quote: It is not.
But the correction is no reprieve.
Shells do not wait for pH 7.

questions.why: In paragraph 10 the author calls the phrase false and calls the imprecision harmful, then immediately says the correction is no reprieve. Both halves of that move belong to the attitude.
distractorNotes: The author calls the imprecision harmful rather than useful.
The author rejects the slogan yet explicitly refuses to treat the correction as a reprieve.
The author gives a full paragraph to why the wording matters, which is not indifference.
The objection is that the phrase overstates what is happening to pH, not that it understates it.

questions.stem: In the discussion of the ancient warming interval, the author's attitude toward that record as evidence is best described as
choices: appreciative of what it shows and wary of how far it is stretched
convinced that it settles the question of how fast the present change is moving
skeptical that an event of that kind occurred in the way described
impatient with the scientists who spend their careers reading sediment cores
confident that modern proxies have removed what uncertainty once remained

proof.quote: The event is instructive
asked with some regularity to carry more weight than it can bear
What it does not show is the present rate.

questions.why: Paragraph 15 opens by calling the event instructive and also asked to carry more weight than it can bear, then lists what it cannot show: the present rate, a single decade, and pH values free of proxy uncertainty.
distractorNotes: The passage says the opposite, that what the record does not show is the present rate.
The author treats the event as well recorded and genuinely instructive.
The author draws on that work respectfully and questions only how it gets used.
The passage says the proxy values carry real uncertainty.

questions.stem: The passage supports all of the following statements EXCEPT:
choices: Dissolved calcium in seawater changes far less than dissolved carbonate does
A shell can be at risk in water that is still alkaline by ordinary measures
Open ocean pH is expected to fall below neutral within the coming century
Sediment cores cannot resolve a change that lasts only a few decades
Some organisms raise the pH of an internal fluid in order to build their skeletons

proof.quote: Calcium is abundant and varies little
can cross below one while the water is still alkaline
a fifty year event can smear into invisibility
holding its pH well above the pH outside
No plausible emissions trajectory takes the open ocean below 7.

questions.why: Paragraph 10 states the opposite of this choice: no plausible emissions trajectory takes the open ocean below 7. Each of the other four traces back to a specific line elsewhere in the passage.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 says calcium is abundant and varies little, which is why omega tracks carbonate.
Paragraph 10 makes exactly this point when it says shells do not wait for pH 7.
Paragraph 15 says a fifty year event can smear into invisibility in a core.
Paragraph 11 describes calcifiers pumping hydrogen ions out of a calcifying fluid to hold its pH up.

questions.stem: In which paragraph does the passage describe habitats whose surrounding water chemistry departs from the open ocean pattern?
choices: paragraph 6
paragraph 9
paragraph 11
paragraph 13
paragraph 15

proof.quote: can lift the local saturation state enough to shelter the animals
Estuaries swing across a wider chemical range in a day

questions.why: Paragraph 13 is the one about local settings. Seagrass meadows and kelp forests lift the saturation state around them during daylight, and estuaries swing across a wider chemical range in a day than the open ocean is projected to cross in a century.
distractorNotes: That paragraph maps how saturation changes with depth and between ocean basins, not between habitats.
That paragraph sorts organisms by which crystal form they build.
That paragraph covers chemistry an organism controls inside itself, not the water around it.
That paragraph weighs what the geological record can and cannot show.
